title: Two-day EP for emergency treatment of GTN
context_label: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia with acute illness
schedule_label: Both medicines on days 1 and 2. The specialist may repeat the block weekly for 1–3 weeks.
schedule_summary: Both medicines on days 1 and 2. The specialist may repeat the block weekly for 1–3 weeks. The GTN team decides when to switch to EMA/CO or EMA/EP, combinations of chemotherapy medicines used after induction.
purpose: This short first treatment aims to bring the disease under control while your hospital team stabilises you and prepares the next treatment.
indication_text: Emergency induction for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) with acute illness from liver or central nervous system involvement. Large lung metastases can put breathing at particular risk.
administration_text: Treatment starts urgently in hospital. On each treatment day etoposide runs into a vein over about one hour, followed by cisplatin over about two hours. Extra fluid before cisplatin helps protect the kidneys.
monitoring_summary: Blood counts and kidney and liver tests are repeated. The team checks hCG on day 1 of each cycle and more often if needed.
review_status: Feasibility build. Independent clinical, pharmacy and patient review pending.

agents.name: Etoposide
agents.explanation: Stops dividing cells repairing breaks in their DNA.
agents.mechanism: Stops dividing cells repairing breaks in their DNA.
agents.watch: Tell the nurse at once if you feel faint, hot or breathless during the infusion.
risks: Infusion reaction or low blood pressure
symptoms: Infusion reaction or low blood pressure
visual: Stops dividing cells repairing breaks in their DNA.

agents.name: Cisplatin
agents.explanation: Joins strands of DNA together so dividing cancer cells cannot copy their DNA normally.
agents.mechanism: Joins strands of DNA together so dividing cancer cells cannot copy their DNA normally.
agents.watch: Report ringing ears, trouble hearing, tingling, reduced urine or vomiting that prevents drinking.
visual: Joins strands of DNA together so dividing cancer cells cannot copy their DNA normally.

common_effects.title: What you may notice
common_effects.text: Tiredness, changes in appetite and nausea can affect meals and daily activity. Tell your team early if you are eating or drinking less.

common_effects.title: At home
common_effects.text: Hair loss and a sore mouth can occur. Ask for mouth care or dietary advice before eating and drinking become difficult.

serious_effects.title: Hearing changes · Cisplatin
serious_effects.text: Report ringing or muffled hearing before the next infusion. Changes can persist.

serious_effects.title: Kidney injury · Cisplatin
serious_effects.text: Tell the team if you pass much less urine or cannot keep drinks down.

serious_effects.title: Nerve changes · Cisplatin
serious_effects.text: Report new tingling, numb feet or difficulty with buttons.

serious_effects.title: Infection or bleeding · Etoposide
serious_effects.text: Call urgently for fever, shivering, bleeding that will not stop or feeling suddenly unwell.

serious_effects.title: Infusion reaction · Etoposide
serious_effects.text: During the infusion tell the nurse immediately about tight breathing, dizziness or flushing.

serious_effects.title: Sore mouth · Etoposide
serious_effects.text: Report painful ulcers or difficulty drinking so the team can help.

phases.label: Day 1 · start emergency EP
phases.detail: Your team monitors your breathing, blood pressure and fluid balance during both infusions.

phases.label: Day 2 · continue emergency EP
phases.detail: Both medicines are given again. Bring the anti-sickness record from yesterday so the team can check the doses already given.

questions.q: Why is the first treatment only two days?
questions.a: Your team can begin treating the disease while you are acutely unwell. They reassess your breathing, organ function and hormone results before choosing the next combination.

questions.q: What happens after this part of treatment?
questions.a: The GTN team decides when to switch to EMA/CO or EMA/EP, combinations of chemotherapy medicines used after induction.

Tell ward staff immediately about new breathlessness, coughing blood, a severe headache, confusion or a seizure. At home, call 112 or 999 for severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure. Call the oncology number urgently for fever or shaking chills.

questions.q: Why do I still need the hormone test?
questions.a: GTN cells can produce a hormone called human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). Changes in its level help your specialist see how treatment is working, and follow-up tests can pick up an increase before symptoms appear.

timeline.label: Etoposide and cisplatin
timeline.text: Both infusions on each of days 1–2, with IV fluid before cisplatin.

timeline.label: Dated anti-sickness course
timeline.text: Use the signed schedule for treatment and the two days afterwards.

timeline.label: Recovery and review
timeline.text: No scheduled EP infusion. Your symptoms or blood tests may need attention on any day.

day_groups.title: Recovery and review
day_groups.body: No scheduled EP infusion. Your symptoms or blood tests may need attention on any day.
day_groups.action: Call urgently for a fever or if suddenly unwell.

support.title: Etoposide
support.text: Tell the nurse at once if you feel faint, hot or breathless during the infusion.

support.title: Cisplatin
support.text: Report ringing ears, trouble hearing, tingling, reduced urine or vomiting that prevents drinking.

support.title: Fluids and nausea
support.text: Kidney-protecting fluid is given before cisplatin. Follow your dated anti-sickness plan and call if vomiting prevents drinking.

support.title: Gaps between treatment visits
support.text: Keep your 24-hour oncology number and treatment card with you. Report fever or sudden illness straight away, including at night and during a break.

teachback: Can you point to the next infusion date, show which anti-sickness doses you already took and find the 24-hour number?
consent_support: Discuss the risk from rapidly progressive disease, the short induction course, the next chemotherapy combination, effects on fertility and the need for hCG follow-up.

evidence.title: Low-dose EP induction in high-risk GTN
evidence.interpretation: A specialist centre reported fewer early deaths in a later group of people treated for high-risk disease. In that group, doctors selected some of the people most seriously ill for short induction chemotherapy.
evidence.limitations: Hospital care also changed over time. The study cannot tell us exactly how much of the improvement came from the two-day treatment.

monitoring_schedule.title: Tests and timing

rows.label: At admission
cells: Blood count, kidney and liver tests and a blood pregnancy-hormone test (hCG) help the team assess illness and plan treatment.
Tell the team about ringing in the ears, hearing loss or tingling. Hearing tests and a measured kidney clearance may be needed.

rows.label: During induction
cells: Blood counts and kidney and liver tests are repeated. The team checks hCG on day 1 of each cycle and more often if needed.
If a third block is planned, ask about the 24-hour urine collection used to measure kidney clearance beforehand.

rows.label: After remission and consolidation
cells: The NCCP schedule checks hCG every two weeks for six months, monthly for six months, then every two months for two years.
Get your own testing dates and specialist contact details before leaving hospital.

monitoring_schedule.note: Your team records the dates and arranges extra tests if your symptoms or results change.
